head: Open source vs closed source password managers: what it means for you
dek: An open source password manager lets anyone read its code, while a closed source one relies on audits by firms it hires; either way, your master password and two-factor sign-in decide most of how safe your vault is.

p: Open source means the app's code is public. Bitwarden says its code is on GitHub and anyone can review, audit and contribute to it. Proton says all Proton Pass apps are open source, and KeePassXC is published under the GPLv3 licence and is free.

Closed source means only the company sees the full code. 1Password wrote in its own glossary on 12 June 2026 that it isn't open source, although it uses open source parts and has published some, such as a passkey library.

The argument for open source is that more people can look for mistakes, and 1Password's own post agrees that public code can help bugs get found and fixed faster. Open code still needs experts to read it: Bitwarden says it also pays Cure53 for regular security audits and penetration tests.

The argument from the closed side is that open projects can be attacked through their contributors. 1Password's post points to the XZ incident of 2024, when a backdoor was slipped into an open source Linux tool, and to volunteer apps that don't get regular updates. Instead, 1Password relies on outside audits, penetration testing and a bug bounty, and says it publishes the results of independent audits.

A bigger difference for everyday use is where the vault is kept. Bitwarden, Proton Pass and 1Password sync an encrypted vault through the company's servers, so it's on all your devices. Proton says your data is encrypted with 256-bit AES-GCM and only you can decrypt it.

KeePassXC works the other way: it keeps an encrypted file on your own computer, with no cloud part of its own, on Windows, Mac and Linux. You can put that file in a cloud folder you choose, but syncing it is up to you. Its version 2.7.9 received a first-level security certification from France's cyber agency ANSSI.

sections.h: What a real attack looked like this year
p: On 31 May 2026, the password manager Dashlane acknowledged an attack in which someone flooded its device sign-up system with automated requests. According to Help Net Security, the attacker got past two-factor checks for fewer than 20 personal plan customers, added a new device to their accounts and downloaded copies of their vaults.

Those copies stayed encrypted and need each user's master password to open, and Dashlane said it found no sign that its internal systems were breached. Help Net Security pointed out that a weak master password could still be cracked offline: that risk sits with the password, whatever the app's code.

Bitwarden wrote on 4 November 2026 that its redesigned app, in beta since September for the Chrome extension and the Windows and Mac apps, is due to reach all cloud users in November. Since July, Bitwarden on Android 10 and newer can move passkeys to and from other apps that support the FIDO Alliance's exchange standard, as it already could on iOS 26.
On 11 November, DuckDuckGo's Windows browser started accepting password manager extensions, beginning with Bitwarden and LastPass.

means: Open source lets outside experts check the code; closed source asks you to trust the company and its auditors. For most people, a long unique master password and two-factor sign-in matter more than which kind they pick.
todo: Whichever password manager you use, make the master password long and used nowhere else, turn on two-factor sign-in, and check the company's security page for its latest published audit.
